abstract: Plant species differ widely in their sensitivity to ammonium, and legumes are generally more sensitive than cereals, yet the mechanisms behind this difference remain unclear. Photorespiration links photosynthetic carbon assimilation with nitrogen metabolism, but its response to nitrogen form has rarely been compared between species. We grew the legume Medicago truncatula, with and without rhizobia, and the cereal wild emmer wheat (Triticum dicoccoides) under nitrate or ammonium, and measured gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, leaf nitrogen, carbon isotope composition and amino acid profiles. Ammonium reduced biomass in both species, but through different leaf-level responses. In M. truncatula, ammonium increased leaf nitrogen but decreased CO2 assimilation, electron transport and photorespiratory CO2 release, lowering photosynthetic nitrogen-use efficiency. These effects were strongest in rhizobia-inoculated plants. In T. dicoccoides, ammonium increased photorespiration and photosystem II operating efficiency, photosynthesis and photosynthetic nitrogen-use efficiency were maintained, and nitrogen accumulated in asparagine and arginine-pathway amino acids. Photorespiration therefore responded in opposite directions to the same nitrogen form in the two species. We propose that sustained photorespiration helps maintain leaf carbonnitrogen coordination under ammonium, whereas its suppression marks leaf-level ammonium sensitivity, with implications for efforts to engineer photorespiration in crops.
